blocks.text: The opening stages of the voyage are marked by named locations: the party is bound for Italy, sails under Cyprus, reaches Myra, struggles near Cnidus, and coasts along Crete to Fair Havens, near Lasea. These names trace a difficult journey rather than a simple sequence of stops; the passage distinguishes destinations, places passed near, and places actually reached.

The chapter itself makes changing winds and difficult navigation central to the unfolding danger. Reading the locations according to their distinct roles—destination, nearby point, or actual stop—clarifies why the voyage becomes increasingly precarious without adding details beyond the narrative.

Acts 27 contains detailed knowledge of Mediterranean sailing, but two questions remain unsettled: the precise location of the wreck and how directly the first-person account reflects eyewitness dependence. The narrative’s detail should therefore be noticed without claiming more certainty than the evidence permits.

sections.title: A Question of Detail and Perspective

blocks.text: Acts survives in early papyri and major Greek manuscripts, including P45, P53, P74, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Bezae; these preserve different portions and textual profiles. Historical assessment of Acts is best made claim by claim, comparing particular statements with independent evidence rather than assigning the whole work a blanket label of reliable or unreliable.

Acts uses first-person plural narration in several sections, including Acts 27–28, but what this implies about authorship or sources remains disputed. Codex Bezae and related witnesses also preserve a notably distinctive form of Acts, so individual textual readings require case-by-case judgment.

sections.title: Acts as a Preserved and Interpreted Work
